pr_title: sql: implement an interlock to modify unsafe settings
pr_body:
Fixes #109810.
Epic: CRDB-28893

As discussed [here](https://docs.google.com/document/d/11mWsfORExZxKqyMJfa6vg7LUzLEYhJ295NkaP1-bvL4/edit?disco=AAAA3lp44WY).

Prior to this patch, it was possible to easily automate `SET CLUSTER
SETTING` for unsafe cluster settings. This is undesirable; we want to
strongly incentivize a human operator paying attention to changes to
these settings.

This patch implements an *interlock*: a mechanism through which the
operator needs to perform two concurrent, related actions for the
change to take effect.

This works as follows:

1. the operator attempts to change a cluster setting from a SQL shell,
   for example:

   ```sql
   SET CLUSTER SETTING kv.raft_log.synchronization.unsafe.disabled = true;
   ```

2. the server fails the execution, with an error:

   ```
   ERROR: changing cluster setting
   "kv.raft_log.synchronization.unsafe.disabled" may cause cluster
   instability or data corruption. To confirm the change, run the
   following command before trying again:

   SET unsafe_setting_interlock_key = 'B7TxIA==';

   ```

3. the operator can then perform the recommended action, then
   try SET CLUSTER SETTING again. Because the key is properly
   set, the SET CLUSTER SETTING statement succeeds.

Also, `RESET` statements (or `SET CLUSTER SETTING ... = DEFAULT`) are
not subject to the interlock, as we assume that the default value is
safe for use.
pr_comments: This change is [](https://reviewable.io/reviews/cockroachdb/cockroach/109801)
planning to add a few unit tests after initial convo

I'm happy to see increased protections placed on these truly unsafe settings, that arguably shouldn't even exist, but which we've found useful for some reason or another (a break-glass recovery tool, a benchmarking tool, etc) and thus begrudgingly keep around.

That said, I might suggest a slightly simpler mechanism here, that doesn't use an an additional persisted setting slot, and doesn't require a separate session, as that seems like It could make it difficult to use in automated testing (which is one place where we would have legitimate use for unsafe settings). 

Perhaps we could just reject setting any unsafe setting unless a local session variable in the session is set to something that allows it. e.g. 
```
SET DEBUG_ENABLE_UNSAFE_SETTINGS = <something>
SET CLUSTER SETTING x.unsafe_y.enabled = true # succeeds only when prior session var set
```

`something` here could be a simple true/false, or could be something more complex, like a comma-separated allowlist, or  could be an opaque key like the one used in your multi-setting approach just switched to a session var. We could also give this its own syntax, like  `ALTER SETTING ENABLE UNSAFE;` that does a bit more than set a session var: it could emit an event log entry in the process of setting the session var, so there is record someone is in going into the danger zone, and could also enable audit logging or something, so that we have a log of every stmt run while in an unsafe session.

A session var/mode is likely how we'll gate access to system and internal tables in the future, so such an approach could be consistent with that when we do it.

> I might suggest a slightly simpler mechanism here, that doesn't use an an additional persisted setting slot, and doesn't require a separate session, as that seems like It could make it difficult to use in automated testing (which is one place where we would have legitimate use for unsafe settings).

I have thought long and deep about whether a session var would be useful here, and I believe it's not the right choice:

- if the mechanism is as simple as "a session var needs to be set", then we're defeating the point of the interlock by making folk able to automate it easily.
- we already have two reliable mechanisms for use in tests: setting overrides, and env var defaults. I have updated the  existing test code in this PR accordingly to illustrate my point. So it's not clear to me that we need anything else.

> A session var/mode is likely how we'll gate access to system and internal tables in the future, so such an approach could be consistent with that when we do it.

I don't feel that the two things here are necessarily related, so I don't feel they need to be consistent with each other. And then, even if we found them related, I could also see use of a more intense interlock for access to system tables too. Open to change opinions.

> if the mechanism is as simple as "a session var needs to be set", then we're defeating the point of the interlock by making folk able to automate it easily.

We could still do a unique key mechanism like you've constructed that is somewhat resistant to blind automation, just using a session var instead of a persisted second setting.
 e.g. 
```
> SET CLUSTER SETTING some_unsafe_setting = 1;
ERROR: setting some_unsafe_setting is unsafe; if you are sure you wish to set it, run SET debug_enable_unsafe = '3c2daf8' in this session and then try again

> SET debug_enable_unsafe = '3c2daf8';
SET

> SET CLUSTER SETTING some_unsafe_setting = 1;
SET
```

In this flow, 3c2daf8 could be e.g. hash of the session UUID and the unsafe setting name, that way the token isn't reusable in any future session, and requires seeing the strong warning error the first time.

> In this flow, 3c2daf8 could be e.g. hash of the session UUID and the unsafe setting name, that way the token isn't reusable in any future session, and requires seeing the strong warning error the first time.

Thank you i will mull it over.

My motivation with my suggestions are that I'd a) prefer to avoid using an additional persisted setting if possible, particularly not one per unsafe setting and b) the timer/concurrent aspect seems complicated to explain and test; a client that hides notices would hang for 3 minutes which is kinda unfortunate. I think we get most of the same benefit -- of confirming you've seen the warning and want to do it anyway -- with a unique token in a single session var.

Updated as requested. Also now ready with tests.

PTAL

Just backfilling some discussion we had outside the issue:

>  then we're defeating the point of the interlock by making folk able to automate it easily.

I'm 100% on board with making sure that users need to make a purposeful and informed decision before using an unsafe setting.  However, making something difficult to automate does come at a cost. Once the user has decided that they need to use such a setting, they should be able to reliably integrate that decision into the tools they use for the management of their infrastructure.  If they can't, the ability to start new infrastructure that depends on CRDB may become unreliable or may depend on steps that exist outside of their standard configuration management tooling and thus not be subject to ongoing code review, testing, etc.

As you mentioned, in this case, there is an alternative: use the environment variable.

If this setting didn't happen to have an environment variable, it looks to me like the user would be required to do something like issue the `SET CLUSTER SETTING` command, parse the error output, issue the `SET` command, and then issues the `SET CLUSTER SETTING` command again. This is possible and certainly better than having to open another session. But I do wonder if we need something better for the user to do than attempting to parse the error message.

That said, if we reserve the `unsafe` moniker for truly unsafe settings, then their use by users in production should be incredibly rare. Because of that rarity, I don't think my concern here needs to block this as a feature.

Should the WithUnsafe option perhaps conflict with the WithPublic option?

This is checked by the linter.

> This is checked by the linter.

Ah, missed this, thanks!

> something better for the user to do than attempting to parse the error message.

If we find that the error string parsing is too much friction, we can always come back later and add a builtin to generate the token for you, so you can signal that you know you're about to set an unsafe setting, e.g.  e.g. `SET .. = crdb_allow_unsafe_setting_in_session('some.unsafe.setting')`. That said, I don't think we need to do this now, or perhaps ever -- if someone complains about the slight crudeness of error string parsing, rather than the unsafe behavior itself, they might be focusing on the wrong thing. If extracting a token from error string is a little uncomfortable, and adds a bit of friction to setting one of these, that feels like a good thing in my book.
